questions.question: What does the `_transport_for_url` method in `httpx/_client.py` do, and what does it return when no mount pattern matches the URL?
questions.ground_truth: CORRECTED (ground-truth audit, verified against real source in httpx/_client.py and httpx/_utils.py): iterates self._mounts and returns the first transport whose URL pattern matches; falls back to self._transport (the default pool) when no pattern matches. IMPORTANT: self._mounts is NOT iterated in raw insertion order -- Client.__init__ explicitly re-sorts it via `self._mounts = dict(sorted(self._mounts.items()))`, and URLPattern (httpx/_utils.py) defines a real priority() method (port specificity, then hostname length, then scheme length) used for this sort -- its own docstring states "The priority allows URLPattern instances to be sortable, so that we can match from most specific to least specific." Original ground truth incorrectly claimed plain insertion order; corrected after the system's own answer (grounded in real source) contradicted it and was independently verified against httpx/_utils.py directly.

questions.question: What three connection-count parameters does the `Limits` class control, and what is the default value of each?
questions.ground_truth: max_connections (100), max_keepalive_connections (20), keepalive_expiry (5 seconds). Verifiable in httpx/_config.py.

questions.question: What is `ASGITransport`, and what two use cases does the official documentation explicitly identify for it?
questions.ground_truth: A transport that sends requests directly into an ASGI application without a network hop. Documented use cases: (1) using httpx as a test client inside test suites, (2) mocking external services in dev/staging environments. Verifiable in docs/advanced/transports.md.

questions.question: What does `BaseClient.build_request()` return, and at what point in the request lifecycle is it called relative to actually sending the request?
questions.ground_truth: Returns an httpx.Request object. It is called before the send step -- it constructs and merges all request parameters (method, URL, headers, content, timeout) into a finalized Request that can then be passed to send() or async_send(). Verifiable in httpx/_client.py.

questions.question: What does the `mounts` parameter on `httpx.Client.__init__` accept, and what is the type of its keys vs its values?
questions.ground_truth: A dictionary where keys are URL pattern strings (e.g. "https://", "all://", "http://example.com") and values are transport instances (subclasses of BaseTransport) or None (which disables the transport for that pattern). Verifiable in httpx/_client.py and docs.

questions.question: How does httpx support both asyncio and trio as async backends without statically importing or coupling to either at module load time?
questions.ground_truth: httpx delegates all async primitives (sleep, Event, locks) to httpcore, which does runtime detection -- it checks at call time which async library is running (using sniffio) and dispatches accordingly. httpx itself does not import asyncio or trio directly for this purpose. Verifiable via httpcore dependency and httpx/_transports/.

questions.question: How does httpx's streaming response (`client.stream(...)`) prevent the entire response body from being loaded into memory before the caller accesses it?
questions.ground_truth: stream() is a context manager that wraps send(..., stream=True). The transport returns a SyncByteStream / AsyncByteStream object rather than a fully-read bytes body. The response body is only read from the socket as the caller iterates response.iter_bytes() or similar. The connection is returned to the pool only when the context manager exits (or response.close() is called). Verifiable in httpx/_client.py and httpx/_models.py.

questions.question: How does httpx determine priority when two mount patterns both match a URL -- for example, `"https://"` and `"https://example.com"`?
questions.ground_truth: CORRECTED (ground-truth audit): httpx DOES sort mounts by specificity, via URLPattern.priority() (httpx/_utils.py) -- a tuple of (port_priority, host_priority, scheme_priority) where more specific patterns (explicit port, longer hostname, longer scheme) sort first. Client.__init__ applies this sort explicitly: `self._mounts = dict(sorted(self._mounts.items()))`. _transport_for_url then iterates the already-sorted dict and returns the first match, so the MORE SPECIFIC pattern (e.g. "https://example.com") naturally wins over a less specific one ("https://") without any extra logic at match time -- the specificity ordering happens once, at construction. Original ground truth incorrectly claimed httpx relies on plain insertion order with no priority mechanism; corrected after direct source verification (URLPattern.priority()'s own docstring: "The priority allows URLPattern instances to be sortable, so that we can match from most specific to least specific.").

questions.question: How does httpx's `Timeout` class allow different timeout durations for connect, read, write, and pool-acquire operations independently on a single request?
questions.ground_truth: Timeout stores four separate values (connect, read, write, pool). When a timeout value is passed as a plain number to the client constructor, it is applied to all four fields. The transport then reads the appropriate field at each I/O stage. Verifiable in httpx/_config.py and httpx/_transports/.

questions.question: How does `httpx.Client` handle thread safety for concurrent requests from multiple threads sharing the same client instance?
questions.ground_truth: Thread safety is enforced at the transport/connection-pool layer (in httpcore), not at the Client class level. Client itself does not add threading locks around its own state, by explicit design choice. The pool uses locks internally to manage connection acquisition. Verifiable via Discussion #1633 and httpcore internals. Note: Client cannot be shared across multiple event loops in async mode because the underlying connection pool is bound to one loop.

questions.question: Where in the codebase is the logic that merges per-request `auth` with the client-level default `auth`?
questions.ground_truth: BaseClient._build_auth() (line 445-455) and BaseClient._build_request_auth() (line 457-473) in httpx/_client.py -- these are the actual merge/resolution methods. BaseClient.build_request() (line 340-389) is the higher-level orchestrator that calls them, not the merge logic itself. Request-level auth is checked first, falling back to self.auth.

questions.question: Where does httpx decode response content according to the charset advertised in the `Content-Type` header?
questions.ground_truth: CORRECTED (ground-truth audit, verified against real source in httpx/_models.py): the text property on the Response class, but the actual mechanism is NOT a bare self.content.decode(self.encoding) call as originally claimed -- it uses a dedicated TextDecoder class: `decoder = TextDecoder(encoding=self.encoding or "utf-8"); self._text = "".join([decoder.decode(self.content), decoder.flush()])`. This same TextDecoder is shared with the streaming iter_text()/aiter_text() methods, which is why it's a dedicated class rather than an inline decode call.

questions.question: Where is the URL pattern matching logic for mounts implemented -- specifically, the code that decides whether `"https://"` matches `https://example.com/path`?
questions.ground_truth: CORRECTED (ground-truth audit, verified against real source): the URLPattern class lives in httpx/_utils.py (not _urlparse.py or _urls.py as originally guessed). Its matches(url) method does the prefix-matching check; its separate priority() method (also real, confirmed) computes a specificity-based sort key used by Client.__init__ to order self._mounts before _transport_for_url ever iterates it -- so pattern matching and pattern PRIORITY are two distinct, both-real mechanisms on the same class.

questions.question: Where does httpx enforce that a closed client cannot send further requests?
questions.ground_truth: Client and AsyncClient track state via an internal ClientState enum (values: UNOPENED, OPENED, CLOSED). The send() / async_send() methods check this state and raise RuntimeError if the client is closed. Verifiable in httpx/_client.py.

questions.question: Where in the source does the retry logic live for httpx -- and if it doesn't exist at the `httpx` layer, where does it live and how is it exposed to users?
questions.ground_truth: Retry logic does NOT exist at the httpx layer at all. It lives in httpcore (the transport layer) and is surfaced to httpx users only via httpx.HTTPTransport(retries=N) or httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(retries=N), which pass the value down to httpcore's connection pool. httpx itself has no retry code. Verifiable in httpx/_transports/default.py.

questions.question: Why was sync support completely dropped in httpx 0.8, and what specific problems with the original approach caused it to be removed?
questions.ground_truth: Issue #572. The original approach bridged sync onto async using subclassing (Sync*/Async* variants inheriting from Base* classes). Two specific failure modes: (1) the subclassing produced poorer, less comprehensible code; (2) environment incompatibilities, specifically being unable to run in some environments where top-level async support was provided (e.g. failing under Jupyter). The fix was the unasync code-generation approach, producing pure sync and pure async implementations rather than a bridged hybrid.

questions.question: Why was the transport layer factored out into a separate `httpcore` library rather than kept as internal httpx code?
questions.ground_truth: Documented across multiple httpx issues and the httpcore README. The split exists so that (a) the low-level HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 send primitive is reusable by other projects without pulling in httpx's higher-level concerns (cookies, redirects, auth, user-friendly config); and (b) the two layers can evolve independently, with httpcore being stable and httpx iterating faster on its API surface.

questions.question: Why was the transport API redesigned to expose `httpx.HTTPTransport` (wrapping httpcore) rather than requiring users to instantiate `httpcore.SyncConnectionPool` directly for custom transport configuration?
questions.ground_truth: Issue #1274 and Issue #1173. Users needing any custom transport configuration had to instantiate httpcore.SyncConnectionPool directly, meaning specifying all the defaults that httpx would normally set -- subject to change across releases, a maintenance burden. The fix (httpx.HTTPTransport wrapping httpcore) lets users override just the specific parameter they care about while inheriting all other httpx-managed defaults automatically.

questions.question: Why does the transport API use context managers (`with transport.handle_request(request) as response`) rather than a simpler `response = transport.request(request)` + explicit `response.close()` call pattern?
questions.ground_truth: Discussion #1530. Context managers give a structural guarantee that the response stream is consumed and the connection is released, which a plain close() callback approach can't enforce -- callers can forget to call close(), leading to resource leaks and connection pool exhaustion. The cost (stack traces showing interleaved __enter__ calls) was considered acceptable relative to the correctness guarantee.

questions.question: Why does `AsyncClient` explicitly not support sharing a connection pool across multiple asyncio event loops?
questions.ground_truth: Discussion #1633. The connection pool in httpcore binds socket handles and async primitives (locks, events) to a specific event loop at creation time. Sharing the pool across loops would require thread-safe cross-loop coordination of those primitives, adding complexity and subtle race condition risk. The deliberate design choice is to keep the pool loop-bound and let the caller manage one client per loop.

questions.question: Why does httpx default to strict timeouts (5s connect, 5s read) rather than the no-timeout default that the `requests` library uses?
questions.ground_truth: Documented in httpx's design philosophy in the README and docs. Production HTTP clients that don't set timeouts are a common source of hung processes and hard-to-diagnose failures. The requests no-timeout default is cited as a known footgun. httpx makes strict timeouts everywhere a design principle rather than an opt-in feature.

questions.question: Why does httpx expose `Client` and `AsyncClient` as sibling classes sharing a `BaseClient` superclass rather than a single class with both sync and async methods on it?
questions.ground_truth: Issue #572 and subsequent design discussions. A single class with mixed sync/async methods was considered and rejected: it makes type signatures ambiguous, forces IDE/type-checker users to mentally track which methods are awaitable, and creates confusion for users who only need one mode. The unasync code-generation approach (two separate clean classes) was preferred for clarity at the cost of some duplication.

questions.question: Why does httpx not implement HTTP response caching (RFC 7234) when other HTTP clients like `got` and `requests-cache` do?
questions.ground_truth: Documented in httpx's FAQ and design docs. Caching is a cross-cutting concern with significant edge cases (cache invalidation, vary headers, conditional requests). Including it in the core library would add complexity and dependency surface for users who don't need it. httpx treats caching as a transport-layer concern -- users can implement a caching transport by subclassing BaseTransport, keeping the core library minimal.

questions.question: Why did the httpx authors choose 5 seconds specifically as the default timeout value for connect and read operations?
questions.ground_truth: No PR, issue, commit, or documentation explains the specific choice of 5 seconds. The value appears in the codebase without a documented rationale for why 5 rather than 3, 10, or 30.

questions.question: Why does httpx name its internal implementation modules with a leading underscore (e.g. `_client.py`, `_config.py`, `_models.py`) while re-exporting all public classes from the top-level `__init__.py`?
questions.ground_truth: This is a Python convention signal for implementation detail, not public API -- but there is no documented httpx-specific reasoning for why they chose this convention over alternatives. A system that just explains the Python convention without acknowledging it's not httpx-specific documented reasoning should score partial credit at most.

questions.question: Why does httpx's URL pattern matching not automatically sort patterns by specificity (most specific first), placing that burden on the caller's insertion order instead?
questions.ground_truth: No documented rationale in PRs, issues, or commits explains this specific design decision. A system that invents a plausible reason without citing a source scores zero.

questions.question: Why did the httpx project choose the name "httpx" rather than alternatives like `http2`, `requests2`, or `async-requests`?
questions.ground_truth: No documented naming rationale found. The name predates the repo's public history in a way that leaves no traceable decision thread.

questions.question: List the exact internal call chain from `httpx.Client.get(url)` to the point where the request is handed off to `httpcore`. Name each function and the file it lives in, in order.
questions.ground_truth: Client.get() [_client.py] -> Client.request() [_client.py] -> Client.send() [_client.py] -> the internal send helper [_client.py] -> transport.handle_request(request) [_transports/default.py] -> httpcore connection pool. The system must show the chain it actually traversed via graph query, not a paraphrase from memory.

questions.question: Which files within the httpx source tree directly import from `httpx/_client.py`?
questions.ground_truth: At minimum httpx/__init__.py (re-exports Client/AsyncClient), possibly httpx/_api.py (convenience functions like httpx.get()). Tests whether reverse-import edges in the graph are populated correctly.

questions.question: Which httpx source files import the `Timeout` class, either directly from `httpx/_config.py` or via `httpx/__init__.py`?
questions.ground_truth: At minimum httpx/_client.py (uses Timeout for request merging), httpx/_transports/default.py (passes timeout to httpcore). Must be derived from graph edges, not recalled.

questions.question: What does `got.extend()` return, and how does it differ from calling `got(url, options)` with inline options?
questions.ground_truth: got.extend(options) returns a new Got instance (a new callable) with the given options merged as persistent defaults. It differs from inline options in that the returned instance carries those defaults for all future calls made through it, rather than applying options only to a single request.

questions.question: What are the six hook points got exposes, and at what stage of the request lifecycle does each fire?
questions.ground_truth: init (when a Got instance is created / options normalized), beforeRequest (after options are resolved, before the request is sent), beforeRedirect (before following a redirect), beforeRetry (before each retry attempt), afterResponse (after receiving a response, can trigger a retry), beforeError (before a RequestError is thrown). Verifiable in documentation/9-hooks.md. CAVEAT (ground-truth audit, verified against the real, full documentation/9-hooks.md chunk): a 7th real hook, beforeCache, also exists in the current docs (fires right before a response is cached). This ground truth's 'six' framing may be based on an older got version; a system correctly reading the current full docs may reasonably report beforeCache instead of one of the other six, which should not be penalized as wrong without checking which six it actually named and why.

questions.question: What does `got.paginate()` return vs `got.paginate.all()`, and when is each appropriate?
questions.ground_truth: got.paginate() returns an async iterator -- consumed one page item at a time with for await. got.paginate.all() returns a Promise resolving to an array of all items across all pages. paginate() is appropriate for large datasets (memory-efficient streaming); paginate.all() is appropriate for small datasets needing all results at once. Verifiable in documentation/4-pagination.md.

questions.question: What does the `calculateDelay` function in got's retry options receive as arguments, and what must it return?
questions.ground_truth: Receives an object containing { error, retryCount, computedValue } (computedValue is got's internally computed delay based on Retry-After headers or exponential backoff). Must return a number (milliseconds to wait before the next retry) or 0 to stop retrying. Verifiable in documentation/7-retry.md and source/ types.

questions.question: What is the `mutableDefaults` option on a got instance, and what problem does it solve?
questions.ground_truth: When mutableDefaults: true is set on a got instance, the defaults.options object on that instance can be mutated directly after creation (e.g. to reset hooks or retry config). Without it, defaults is frozen and direct mutation silently fails. Exists specifically to allow resetting hooks/retry/pagination to defaults without creating a new instance. Verifiable in documentation/2-options.md.

questions.question: How does got determine whether and how long to wait before retrying a failed request -- specifically, what inputs does it use to compute the delay?
questions.ground_truth: got checks (in order): (1) the Retry-After response header, if present; (2) the calculateDelay user function, if provided; (3) its own exponential backoff formula based on retryCount. The retry is only attempted if the error type and HTTP method match the configured retry.methods and retry.errorCodes/retry.statusCodes sets. Verifiable in source/ and documentation/7-retry.md.

questions.question: How does got's `afterResponse` hook enable token-refresh flows -- specifically, how can a hook cause got to retry a 401 response with a new auth token?
questions.ground_truth: The hook receives the response and a retryWithMergedOptions function. If the hook calls and returns retryWithMergedOptions({ headers: { authorization: newToken } }), got retries the original request with the merged options. This retry does not count toward retry.limit. Verifiable in documentation/9-hooks.md.

questions.question: How does got's pagination determine when to stop fetching pages -- what return value from the `paginate` function signals the end of pages?
questions.ground_truth: The paginate function (provided by the caller in pagination.paginate) receives { response, currentItems, allItems } and must return either a new options object for the next page request, or false to signal that pagination should stop. Returning false terminates the async iterator. Verifiable in documentation/4-pagination.md.

questions.question: How does got's hook system handle multiple hooks registered for the same lifecycle event -- are they called sequentially or in parallel, and what is the execution order?
questions.ground_truth: Hooks for the same lifecycle event are stored as arrays and called sequentially (one after another, in registration order, each awaited before the next). Not parallelised. Explicit in got's docs: hooks are given as arrays, thus multiple hooks can be given. Verifiable in documentation/9-hooks.md and source.

questions.question: Where in got's source is the decision made to use the `Retry-After` response header to override the computed retry delay?
questions.ground_truth: In source/core/index.ts or the retry-handling module within source/. The retry delay calculation reads the retry-after response header value and uses it as the delay if present and valid, overriding the local calculation. Verifiable in the retry logic within source/.

questions.question: Where does got merge options when `got.extend()` is called with new defaults -- specifically, how are array-type options like `hooks` merged (replaced vs concatenated)?
questions.ground_truth: In got's options normalization code (likely source/core/options.ts or source/types.ts). Array-type options like hooks.beforeRequest are concatenated (parent hooks + new hooks), not replaced. Non-array options are overwritten. Verifiable in source/ and observable by reading got.extend() behavior in tests.

questions.question: Where does got's code path diverge between returning a Promise (Promise API) and returning a stream (Stream API)?
questions.ground_truth: The divergence happens at the entry point -- got(url, options) returns a GotPromise (which has .json()/.text()/.buffer() methods), while got.stream(url, options) returns a GotStream (which extends Duplex). The split is at the top-level export / factory function. Verifiable in source/index.ts and source/as-promise/index.ts vs source/as-stream/index.ts.

questions.question: Where in got's source is the ESM-only constraint enforced -- i.e., is it a runtime check, a package.json field, or something else?
questions.ground_truth: Enforced via the "type": "module" field in package.json and the absence of any CommonJS build output. There is no runtime check -- the constraint is at the Node.js module-system level. A CommonJS require('got') produces a module-not-found or ESM-interop error from Node itself. Verifiable in package.json.

questions.question: Why did got rewrite its retry functionality in v9 to support HTTP status code retries, and what was the limitation of the v8 approach?
questions.ground_truth: v9 release notes document this explicitly. The v8 approach only retried on some network failures -- errors at the TCP/socket level (ECONNRESET, etc.). It did not retry on HTTP-level failures (e.g. 503 Service Unavailable). The v9 rewrite added retry.statusCodes to enable HTTP-level retry in addition to network-level retry, which is what production API clients typically need.

questions.question: Why was the retry option renamed from `{ retries: function }` to `{ calculateDelay: function }` in v10?
questions.ground_truth: CORRECTED (ground-truth audit, verified against the real, full v10.0.0 release body): the real change was a STRUCTURAL SPLIT, not a simple rename -- the single `retry.retry` option was split into two separate options, `retry.limit` (a number) and `retry.calculateDelay` (a function), per the real release notes' own migrate diff: `retries: 2` -> `limit: 2` and `retries: iteration => ...` -> `calculateDelay: ({attemptCount}) => ...`. IMPORTANT: no "Why:" rationale is given for this specific change in the real release notes -- unlike neighboring bullet points, which do have explicit "Why:" lines. The original ground truth's claimed rationale ("We're trying to reduce the use of null") is REAL TEXT from the v10.0.0 notes, but it is attached to a different, unrelated change two bullet points later ("Use undefined instead of null to omit a header"), not to the retries/calculateDelay split. A system correctly reading the real release notes should find no documented rationale for this specific change and should abstain (unanswerable), not fabricate or misattribute one.

questions.question: Why did got switch to ESM-only from v12 onwards, dropping CommonJS support?
questions.ground_truth: Documented in got's migration guide and related discussion. ESM is the official JavaScript module standard; sindresorhus has publicly stated (across multiple repos) that he believes the Node.js ecosystem should migrate to ESM and that maintaining dual-format builds adds maintenance overhead for no long-term benefit. The breaking change was deliberate and well-signalled.

questions.question: Why does got use `got.extend()` for customization rather than class-based inheritance or a constructor with options?
questions.ground_truth: got itself is a function, not a class -- you can't extend a function via inheritance in a natural way. extend() is the functional composition pattern: it creates a new function that inherits the parent's defaults and merges new ones. This also means multiple extensions can be composed (got.extend(a).extend(b)) without prototype chain complexity.

questions.question: Why does got default `pagination.stackAllItems` to `false` (keeping `allItems` as an empty array in the paginate callback) rather than accumulating all items automatically?
questions.ground_truth: Explicitly documented in documentation/4-pagination.md -- "Setting this to true will significantly increase memory usage when working with a large dataset." The default is false to prevent silent memory exhaustion when paginating large APIs. Users who need allItems for their filter or shouldContinue callbacks must opt in explicitly.

questions.question: Why does got expose `.json()`, `.text()`, and `.buffer()` as methods chained on the returned Promise rather than as separate top-level methods (`got.json()`, `got.text()`, etc.)?
questions.ground_truth: The chained form (got(url).json()) allows a single request to be parsed in different ways without making multiple network requests -- const [json, buffer] = await Promise.all([got(url).json(), got(url).buffer()]) reuses the same underlying request. Top-level methods would not convey this relationship and would make it harder to share a single in-flight request across different response formats. Verifiable in documentation/3-streams.md and source/as-promise/.

questions.question: Why does got use 2 as its default retry limit rather than 1 or 3?
questions.ground_truth: No documented rationale exists for the specific number 2. It appears in documentation/7-retry.md as the default without explanation of why 2 was chosen over other values.

questions.question: Why does got's `beforeError` hook receive a `RequestError` object rather than the raw Node.js error that caused the failure?
questions.ground_truth: No documented rationale is findable in issues or commits for this wrapping decision specifically. Plausible reasons (normalisation, consistent error shape) exist but are not cited in any got source document.

questions.question: Why does got default to treating 408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504 as retryable status codes -- what was the reasoning behind this specific set of status codes in `retry.statusCodes`?
questions.ground_truth: The specific set of status codes is defined in source but the rationale for exactly which codes are included is not documented in any PR, issue, or commit message. A system that infers reasonable HTTP semantics without a source citation scores zero on this question.

questions.question: Why does got name its library "got" -- is the name documented as a reference to HTTP GET, to the past tense of "get" (indicating "retrieved"), or something else?
questions.ground_truth: No documented naming rationale found -- the name predates any traceable decision thread and no issue, PR, or README explains the choice.

questions.question: Which internal got source files directly import from `source/core/errors.ts` (where `RequestError`/`GotError` are defined)?
questions.ground_truth: source/core/response.ts, source/core/options.ts, source/core/index.ts, source/core/diagnostics-channel.ts, source/as-promise/index.ts. Verified directly against source/core/errors.ts via graph query.

questions.question: Trace the call chain from `got(url)` at the top-level entry point down to where the actual Node.js `http.request`/`https.request` is invoked. Name each function and its file.
questions.ground_truth: got() entry [source/index.ts] -> asPromise() [source/as-promise/index.ts] -> the Request constructor / makeRequest [source/core/index.ts] -> Node's http/https.request. Exact chain depends on the got version indexed -- the system must show the path it actually traversed.

questions.ground_truth: source/as-promise/index.ts, source/as-stream/index.ts, and possibly source/index.ts. Must come from the import-edge graph, not a guess.
